newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvia president worried by Russian non-citizens.
newsitem.headline: Latvia president worried by Russian non-citizens.

text.p: The president of the Baltic state of Latvia on Wednesday urged measures to encourage the country's many Russian-speakers to become citizens, an issue which has soured relations with huge neighbour Russia.
Many of Latvia's 700,000 Russian-speakers, mostly ethnic Russians, were barred from automatic citizenship when Latvia won back its independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991.
The issue has badly damaged relations with Moscow, which regularly accuses Latvia of discrimination against Russian-speakers.
President Guntis Ulmanis, in a letter to Prime Minister Andris Shkele, urged that the naturalisation process be made easier.
"It is time to change the state's attitude toward Latvia's residents, who are willing to prove their loyalty to the state, becoming citizens by naturalisation," Ulmanis said.
Ulmanis did not call for fundamental alterations to citizenship laws but wanted changes to make it easier for people to naturalise.
Without citizenship, people cannot vote and are shut out of some state jobs. A naturalisation process exists but of 130,000 eligible so far only 5,000 have applied.
Citizenship is one of the most politcally-sensitive issues in this nation of 2.6 million where ethnic Latvians make up just 52 percent of the population.
Many of Latvia's Russian-speakers arrived during the 50 years of Soviet rule and most Latvians regard them as illegal immigrants or former occupants.
Under Latvian rules, only citizens or descendants of citizens of Latvia before 1940, the year of the Soviet annexation, get automatic citizenship.
Everyone else has to be naturalised, involving exams in Latvian language, history and the constitution.
Ulmanis called for a lower fee for the naturalisation process to three lats ($6) from 30 lats, a large amount when the average monthly wage is around $200.
Ulmanis also wanted students to be exempt from the fee to encourage more young people to apply and the scrapping of a six month limit for people to reapply if they fail the exam.
